newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-UK consumer boom shows no sign of slowing.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-UK consumer boom shows no sign of slowing.

text.p: Britain's consumer boom continued unabated with retail sales surging last month and analysts on Wednesday said this suggested interest rates might have to rise further to stave off inflation.
The Office for National Statistics (ONS) said retail sales rose 0.6 percent over the month in June and were 5.4 percent higher than a year earlier, the same annual increase as in May.

But it was rocketing sales of household goods that caused consternation among financial analysts and propelled the pound to a new seven-and-a-half year high of nearly 3.09 marks on expectations of higher interest rates.
Economists said this was evidence that billions of pounds of "windfall" payments dished out to millions of households by building societies that converted into banks were being spent and not saved.
"The fear that consumer demand is being driven yet higher on the back of windfalls is kept very much alive by the data," said Simon Briscoe, UK economist at Nikko Europe.

Sales of household goods -- consumer durables such as televisions, washing machines and stereo equipment -- leapt by 7.5 percent in June with three-month growth rates reaching levels last seen in the runaway consumer boom of the late 1980s.
"The record rise in household goods fuels the windfall fear and the data reapply upward pressure on interest rates," said Briscoe.

Official interest rates have been raised three times in as many months to stand at 6.75 percent and many economists believe the Bank of England will raise them again in August to try to dampen consumer demand.
However, the decision for policy makers is clouded by the pound's relentless rally, which is punishing firms who depend on selling their goods abroad.
A leading business survey, also released on Wednesday, showed that British exporters were facing their worst summer for five years because of the exchange rate.

The British Chambers of Commerce (BCC) said its quarterly economic survey found overseas orders for both manufacturing and service sector firms slumped in the second quarter to levels last seen in 1992, when Britain was struggling out of recession.
The pound's latest advance, to 3.0878 marks, threatened even more trouble for exporters.
"The survey paints a gloomy picture for exporters, particularly in the smaller business sector," said Ian Peters, deputy director-general of the BCC.
"With interest rates set to increase further, our concern is that sterling will continue to strengthen, causing significant damage to the UK's international competitiveness."
The central bank has said that it is aware of the problems the strong pound is causing.
But minutes from the executive monetary policy committee's June meeting showed monetary policy was not being swayed by the exchange rate.

In June, the committee concluded that delaying the rate rise would not mean the ultimate effect on the exchange rate would be any less, "while the delay would mean some increase in the inflationary risks to the domestic economy".
The Bank's Monetary Policy Committee meets next on August 6 and 7.
